Malicious

/muh-LISH-uhs/ - rhymes with delicious · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Malicious means intended to cause harm; spiteful.

The virus was malicious by design, written to lie quiet for thirty days and then eat the backups first.

Worked Example

Nobody thought much of the loose ribbon until the third shoe failed in a week. Then a stagehand found the razor nicks — tiny, precise, cut where the seam would take the dancer's weight in the lift. A prank ruins a costume; whoever nicked those seams meant for someone to fall.

Malicious is the exact word because it names intent to cause harm. Carelessness could fray a ribbon and bad luck could snap one, but nicks tucked in at the load-bearing seam were chosen. That aim — harm as the point, not the accident — is what separates malicious from thoughtless, and a crime from a prank.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

mean-spirited: Mean-spirited is petty, everyday nastiness — the cutting remark, the small cruelty that costs its target an afternoon. Malicious operates at a different scale and with colder purpose: it plans real harm and means for it to land. A mean-spirited person snipes; a malicious one schemes.

venomous: Venomous is hatred concentrated in words — the poisonous insult, the interview meant to wound, a malicious tongue at work. Malicious is broader: it names any intent to cause harm, whether the weapon is a sentence, a scheme, or a slow campaign.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

kindhearted: wishing others well by instinct

well-meaning: aiming at good, even when it goes wrong

Where it sits · how deliberately the harm is aimed — unkind → malicious → vicious

unkind vs. malicious: Unkind wounds by thoughtlessness or a careless word; malicious takes aim first.

vicious vs. malicious: Vicious goes past malicious — the harm turns savage and stops hiding.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — mal

Root — mal: bad, evil (Latin malus)

Suffix — -icious

Suffix — -icious: full of, given to

Put it together

Put it together: Mal- (bad, evil — Latin malus) + -icious (full of) = full of badness. Latin malitia was wickedness itself; English sharpened it to wickedness with a target. Malicious acts don't merely turn out badly — they were loaded with bad intent before they left the hand.

Use the root in a new word: malfunction

Use the root in a new word: malfunction: A malfunction is a working-badly — the same mal- root diagnosing a machine instead of a motive.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / serious

Malicious is a judgment about intent: the harm was the point. Keep it apart from this unit's odious, which judges the effect — how a thing strikes everyone else — and from retaliation, which at least claims an earlier wrong; malice needs none. If the damage was thoughtless rather than aimed, careless or reckless is the honest charge.
